What is the highest rent Emma will qualify for? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the highest rent Emma will qualify for Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$r =$$ the rent. Step 4. Translate into an inequality. First write a sentence that gives the information to find it. Emma's monthly income must be at least three times the rent. Step 5. Solve the inequality. Remember, $$a > x$$ has the same meaning as $$x < a$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} 5,625 & \geq & {3r} \\ & & \\ 1,875 & \geq & r \\ r & \leq & 1,875 \end{array}$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense. A maximum rent of \$1,875 seems reasonable for an income of \$5,625. Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence. The maximum rent is \$1,875.

title: Example 3.54
snippet: Example 3.54: Dawn won a mini-grant of \$4,000 to buy tablet computers for her classroom. The tablets she would like to buy cost \$254.12 each, including tax and delivery. What is the maximum number of tablets Dawn can buy? Step 1. Read...
body_xml: Dawn won a mini-grant of \$4,000 to buy tablet computers for her classroom. The tablets she would like to buy cost \$254.12 each, including tax and delivery. What is the maximum number of tablets Dawn can buy? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the maximum number of tablets Dawn can buy Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$n =$$ the number of tablets. Step 4. Translate. Write a sentence that gives the information to find it. Translate into an inequality. \$254.12 times the number of tablets is no more than \$4,000. $$254.12n \leq 4,000$$ Step 5. Solve the inequality. But $$n$$ must be a whole number of tablets, so round to 15. $$n \leq 15.74$$ $$n \leq 15$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense. Rounding down the price to \$250, 15 tablets would cost \$3,750, while 16 tablets would be \$4,000. So a maximum of 15 tablets at \$254.12 seems reasonable. Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence. Dawn can buy a maximum of 15 tablets.

title: Example 3.55
snippet: Example 3.55: Pete works at a computer store. His weekly pay will be either a fixed amount, \$925, or \$500 plus 12% of his total sales. How much should his total sales be for his variable pay option to exceed the fixed amount of \$925?...
body_xml: Pete works at a computer store. His weekly pay will be either a fixed amount, \$925, or \$500 plus 12% of his total sales. How much should his total sales be for his variable pay option to exceed the fixed amount of \$925? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the total sales needed for his variable pay option to exceed the fixed amount of \$925 Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$s =$$ the total sales. Step 4. Translate. Write a sentence that gives the information to find it. Translate into an inequality. Remember to convert the percent to a decimal. $$500 + 0.12s > 925$$ Step 5. Solve the inequality. $$\begin{array}{rll} {0.12s} & > & 425 \\ s & > & {3,541.\overset{ \text{—} }{66}} \end{array}$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense. If we round the total sales up to \$4,000, we see that $$500 + 0.12(4,000) = 980$$ , which is more than \$925. Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence. The total sales must be more than \$3,541.67.

title: Example 3.56
snippet: Example 3.56: Sergio and Lizeth have a very tight vacation budget. They plan to rent a car from a company that charges \$75 a week plus \$0.25 a mile. How many miles can they travel and still keep within their \$200 budget? Step 1. Read...
body_xml: Sergio and Lizeth have a very tight vacation budget. They plan to rent a car from a company that charges \$75 a week plus \$0.25 a mile. How many miles can they travel and still keep within their \$200 budget? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the number of miles Sergio and Lizeth can travel Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$m =$$ the number of miles. Step 4. Translate. Write a sentence that gives the information to find it. Translate into an inequality. \$75 plus 0.25 times the number of miles is less than or equal to \$200. $$75 + 0.25m \leq 200$$ Step 5. Solve the inequality. $$\begin{array}{rll} {0.25m} & \leq & 125 \\ m & \leq & {500 \text{miles} } \end{array}$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense. Yes, $$75 + 0.25(500) = 200$$ . Step 7. Write a sentence that answers the question. Sergio and Lizeth can travel 500 miles and still stay on budget.

title: Example 3.57
snippet: Example 3.57: Elliot has a landscape maintenance business. His monthly expenses are \$1,100. If he charges \$60 per job, how many jobs must he do to earn a profit of at least \$4,000 a month? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what...
body_xml: Elliot has a landscape maintenance business. His monthly expenses are \$1,100. If he charges \$60 per job, how many jobs must he do to earn a profit of at least \$4,000 a month? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the number of jobs Elliot needs Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent it. Let $$j =$$ the number of jobs. Step 4. Translate Write a sentence that gives the information to find it. \$60 times the number of jobs minus \$1,100 is at least \$4,000. Translate into an inequality. Step 5. Solve the inequality. Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense.If Elliot did 90 jobs, his profit would be $$60(90) - 1,100$$ , or $$\$ 4,300$$ . This is more than $$\$ 4,000$$ . Step 7. Write a sentence that answer the question. Elliot must work at least 85 jobs.

title: Example 3.58
snippet: Example 3.58: Brenda’s best friend is having a destination wedding and the event will require 3 nights in a hotel. Brenda has \$500 in savings and can earn \$15 an hour babysitting. She expects to pay \$350 airfare, \$375 for food and...
body_xml: Brenda’s best friend is having a destination wedding and the event will require 3 nights in a hotel. Brenda has \$500 in savings and can earn \$15 an hour babysitting. She expects to pay \$350 airfare, \$375 for food and entertainment and \$60 a night for her share of a hotel room. How many hours must she babysit to have enough money to pay for the trip? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. the number of hours Brenda must babysit Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$h =$$ the number of hours. Step 4. Translate.Write a sentence that gives the information to find it. Translate into an inequality. The expenses must be less than or equal to the income. The cost of airfare plus the cost of food and entertainment and the hotel bill must be less than or equal to the savings plus the amount earned babysitting. $$\$350 + \$375 + \$60(3) \leq \$500 + \$15h$$ Step 5. Solve the inequality. $$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ 905 & \leq & {500 + 15h} \\ 405 & \leq & {15h} \\ 27 & \leq & h \\ h & \geq & 27 \end{array}$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense. We substitute 27 into the inequality. $$\begin{array}{l} { 905 \leq 500 + 15h} \\ { 905 \leq 500 + 15(27)} \\ { 905 \leq 905} \end{array}$$ Step 7. Write a sentence that answers the question. Brenda must babysit at least 27 hours.

snippet: Example 4.1: Plot each point in the rectangular coordinate system and identify the quadrant in which the point is located: ⓐ (-5,4) ⓑ (-3,-4) ⓒ (2,-3) ⓓ (-2,3) ⓔ \left( {3,\frac{5}{2}} \right) . The first number of the coordinate pair is...
body_xml:
<example number="4.1">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Plot each point in the rectangular coordinate system and identify the quadrant in which the point is located:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$(-5,4)$$ ⓑ $$(-3,-4)$$ ⓒ $$(2,-3)$$ ⓓ $$(-2,3)$$ ⓔ $$\left( {3,\frac{5}{2}} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first number of the coordinate pair is the x-coordinate, and the second number is the y-coordinate.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ Since $$x = -5$$ , the point is to the left of the y-axis. Also, since $$y = 4$$ , the point is above the x-axis. The point $$(-5,4)$$ is in Quadrant II.</item>
        <item>ⓑ Since $$x = -3$$ , the point is to the left of the y-axis. Also, since $$y = -4$$ , the point is below the x-axis. The point $$(-3,-4)$$ is in Quadrant III.</item>
        <item>ⓒ Since $$x = 2$$ , the point is to the right of the y-axis. Since $$y = -3$$ , the point is below the x-axis. The point $$(2,-3)$$ is in Quadrant lV.</item>
        <item>ⓓ Since $$x = -2$$ , the point is to the left of the y-axis. Since $$y = 3$$ , the point is above the x-axis. The point $$(-2,3)$$ is in Quadrant II.</item>
        <item>ⓔ Since $$x = 3$$ , the point is to the right of the y-axis. Since $$y = \frac{5}{2}$$ , the point is above the x-axis. (It may be helpful to write $$\frac{5}{2}$$ as a mixed number or decimal.) The point $$\left( {3,\frac{5}{2}} \right)$$ is in Quadrant I. Figure 4.3</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 4.8
snippet: Example 4.8: Find three solutions to the equation y = -3x + 2 . We can substitute any value we want for x or any value for y . Since the equation is in y-form, it will be easier to substitute in values of x . Let’s pick x = 0 , x = 1 , and...

Find three solutions to the equation $$y = -3x + 2$$ . We can substitute any value we want for $$x$$ or any value for $$y$$ . Since the equation is in y-form, it will be easier to substitute in values of $$x$$ . Let’s pick $$x = 0$$ , $$x = 1$$ , and $$x = -1$$ . Substitute the value into the equation. Simplify. Simplify. Write the ordered pair. (0, 2) (1, −1) (−1, 5) Check. $$y = -3x + 2$$ $$y = -3x + 2$$ $$y = -3x + 2$$ $$2 ≟ -3 \cdot 0 + 2$$ $$-1 ≟ -3 \cdot 1 + 2$$ $$5 ≟ -3(-1) + 2$$ $$2 ≟ 0 + 2$$ $$-1 ≟ -3 + 2$$ $$5 ≟ 3 + 2$$ $$2 = 2✓$$ $$-1 = -1✓$$ $$5 = 5✓$$
So, $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,-1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-1,5} \right)$$ are all solutions to $$y = -3x + 2$$ . We show them in Table 4.8. $$y = -3x + 2$$ $$x$$ $$y$$ $$(x,y)$$ 0 2 $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ 1 $$-1$$ $$\left( {1,-1} \right)$$ $$-1$$ 5 $$\left( {-1,5} \right)$$

Find three solutions to the equation $$3x + 2y = 6$$ . We can substitute any value we want for $$x$$ or any value for $$y$$ . Since the equation is in standard form, let’s pick first $$x = 0$$ , then $$y = 0$$ , and then find a third point. Substitute the value into the equation. Simplify. Solve. Write the ordered pair. (0, 3) (2, 0) $$\left( 1,\frac{3}{2} \right)$$
Check. $${3x + 2y = 6}$$ $${3x + 2y = 6}$$ $${3x + 2y = 6}$$ $${3 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 3 ≟ 6}$$ $${3 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 0 ≟ 6}$$ $${3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot \frac{3}{2} ≟ 6}$$ $${0 + 6 ≟ 6}$$ $${6 + 0 ≟ 6}$$ $${3 + 3 ≟ 6}$$ $$6 = 6✓$$ $$6 = 6✓$$ $$6 = 6✓$$
So $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,\frac{3}{2}} \right)$$ are all solutions to the equation $$3x + 2y = 6$$ . We can list these three solutions in Table 4.9. $$3x + 2y = 6$$ $$x$$ $$y$$ $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ 0 3 $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ 2 0 $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ 1 $$\frac{3}{2}$$ $$\left( {1,\frac{3}{2}} \right)$$

title: Example 4.15
snippet: Example 4.15: Graph the equation 2x - 3y = 6 . Find three points that are solutions to the equation. \begin{array}{rll} {2x - 3y} & = & 6 \end{array} First, let x = 0 . \begin{array}{rll} {2(0) - 3y} & = & 6 \end{array} Solve for y ....
body_xml:
Graph the equation $$2x - 3y = 6$$ . Find three points that are solutions to the equation. $$\begin{array}{rll} {2x - 3y} & = & 6 \end{array}$$ First, let $$x = 0$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {2(0) - 3y} & = & 6 \end{array}$$ Solve for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {-3y} & = & 6 \\ y & = & -2 \end{array}$$ Now let $$y = 0$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {2x - 3(0)} & = & 6 \end{array}$$ Solve for $$x$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {2x} & = & 6 \\ x & = & 3 \end{array}$$ We need a third point. Remember, we can choose any value for $$x$$ or $$y$$ . We'll let $$x = 6$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {2(6) - 3y} & = & 6 \end{array}$$ Solve for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {12 - 3y} & = & 6 \\ {-3y} & = & -6 \\ y & = & 2 \end{array}$$
We list the ordered pairs in Table 4.17. Plot the points, check that they line up, and draw the line. See Figure 4.11. $$2x - 3y = 6$$ $$x$$ $$y$$ $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ 0 $$-2$$ $$\left( {0,-2} \right)$$ 3 0 $$\left( {3,0} \right)$$ 6 2 $$\left( {6,2} \right)$$

title: Slope of a Line
snippet: Slope of a Line: The slope of a line of a line is m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } . The rise measures the vertical change and the run measures the horizontal change between two points on the line.
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Slope of a Line" title="Slope of a Line">
    <paragraph>The slope of a line of a line is $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rise measures the vertical change and the run measures the horizontal change between two points on the line.</paragraph>
  </note>

What is the slope of the line on the geoboard shown? Use the definition of slope: $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }.$$ Start at the left peg and count the spaces up and to the right to reach the second peg. The rise is 3. $$m = \frac{3}{ \text{run} }$$ The run is 4. $$m = \frac{3}{4}$$ The slope is $$\frac{3}{4}$$ .
This means that the line rises 3 units for every 4 units of run.

title: Example 4.27

Use a geoboard to model a line with slope $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . To model a line on a geoboard, we need the rise and the run. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Replace $$m$$ with $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . $$\frac{1}{2} = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$
So, the rise is 1 and the run is 2. Start at a peg in the lower left of the geoboard. Stretch the rubber band up 1 unit, and then right 2 units. The hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the rubber band represents a line whose slope is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ .

body_xml:
Use a geoboard to model a line with slope $$\frac{-1}{4}.$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Replace $$m$$ with $$\frac{-1}{4}$$ . $$\frac{-1}{4} = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$
So, the rise is $$-1$$ and the run is 4. Since the rise is negative, we choose a starting peg on the upper left that will give us room to count down. We stretch the rubber band down 1 unit, then go to the right 4 units, as shown. The hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the rubber band represents a line whose slope is $$\frac{-1}{4}$$ .

    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Locate two points on the line whose coordinates are integers.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Starting with the point on the left, sketch a right triangle, with the hypotenuse going from the first point to the second point.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Count the rise and the run on the legs of the triangle.</item>

title: Example 4.30
snippet: Example 4.30: Find the slope of the line shown. Locate two points on the graph whose coordinates are integers. \left( {0,5} \right) and \left( {3,3} \right) Which point is on the left? \left( {0,5} \right) Starting at \left( {0,5} \right)...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line shown. Locate two points on the graph whose coordinates are integers. $$\left( {0,5} \right)$$ and $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ Which point is on the left? $$\left( {0,5} \right)$$ Starting at $$\left( {0,5} \right)$$ , sketch a right triangle to $$\left( {3,3} \right)$$ . Count the rise—it is negative. The rise is $$-2$$ . Count the run. The run is 3. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{-2}{3}$$ Simplify. $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ The slope of the line is $$- \frac{2}{3}$$ .
So $$y$$ decreases by 2 units as $$x$$ increases by 3 units. What if we used the points $$\left( {-3,7} \right)$$ and $$\left( {6,1} \right)$$ to find the slope of the line? The rise would be $$-6$$ and the run would be 9. Then $$m = \frac{-6}{9}$$ , and that simplifies to $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ . Remember, it does not matter which points you use—the slope of the line is always the same.

title: Example 4.31
snippet: Example 4.31: Find the slope of the line shown. Locate two points on the graph whose coordinates are integers. \left( {2,3} \right) and \left( {7,6} \right) Which point is on the left? \left( {2,3} \right) Starting at \left( {2,3} \right)...
body_xml:
Find the slope of the line shown. Locate two points on the graph whose coordinates are integers. $$\left( {2,3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {7,6} \right)$$ Which point is on the left? $$\left( {2,3} \right)$$ Starting at $$\left( {2,3} \right)$$ , sketch a right triangle to $$\left( {7,6} \right)$$ . Count the rise. The rise is 3. Count the run. The run is 5. Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{3}{5}$$ The slope of the line is $$\frac{3}{5}$$ .
This means that $$y$$ increases 5 units as $$x$$ increases 3 units. When we used geoboards to introduce the concept of slope, we said that we would always start with the point on the left and count the rise and the run to get to the point on the right. That way the run was always positive and the rise determined whether the slope was positive or negative. What would happen if we started with the point on the right? Let’s use the points $$\left( {2,3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {7,6} \right)$$ again, but now we’ll start at $$\left( {7,6} \right)$$ . Count the rise. The rise is $$-3$$ . Count the run. It goes from right to left, so it is negative. The run is $$-5$$ . Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values of the rise and run. $$m = \frac{-3}{-5}$$ The slope of the line is $$\frac{-3}{-5}$$ .
It does not matter where you start—the slope of the line is always the same.

snippet: Slope Formula: The slope of the line between two points (x_{1},y_{1}) and (x_{2},y_{2}) is m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}} This is the slope formula. The slope is: \begin{matrix} \\ {y \text{of the second point minus} y \text{of...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Slope Formula" title="Slope Formula">
    <paragraph>The slope of the line between two points $$(x_{1},y_{1})$$ and $$(x_{2},y_{2})$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is the slope formula.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The slope is:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \\ {y \text{of the second point minus} y \text{of the first point} } \\ \text{over} \\ \\ {x \text{of the second point minus} x \text{of the first point.} } \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 4.33
snippet: Example 4.33: Use the slope formula to find the slope of the line between the points \left( {1,2} \right) and \left( {4,5} \right) . We'll call \left( {1,2} \right) point #1 and \left( {4,5} \right) point #2. \left(...
body_xml:
Use the slope formula to find the slope of the line between the points $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {4,5} \right)$$ . We'll call $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ point #1 and $$\left( {4,5} \right)$$ point #2. $$\left( \overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{1,2} \right)\left( \overset{x_{2},y_{2}}{4,5} \right)_{}$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ . Substitute the values. $$y$$ of the second point minus $$y$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{5 - 2}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ . $$x$$ of the second point minus $$x$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{5 - 2}{4 - 1}$$ . Simplify the numerator and the denominator. $$m = \frac{3}{3}$$ . Simplify. $$m = 1$$ .
Let’s confirm this by counting out the slope on a graph using $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ . It doesn’t matter which point you call point #1 and which one you call point #2. The slope will be the same. Try the calculation yourself.

title: Example 4.34
snippet: Example 4.34: Use the slope formula to find the slope of the line through the points \left( {-2,-3} \right) and \left( {-7,4} \right) . We'll call \left( {-2,-3} \right) point #1 and \left( {-7,4} \right) point #2. \left(...
body_xml:
Use the slope formula to find the slope of the line through the points $$\left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-7,4} \right)$$ . We'll call $$\left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ point #1 and $$\left( {-7,4} \right)$$ point #2. $$\left( \overset{x_{1},y_{1}}{-2,-3} \right)\left( \overset{x_{2},y_{2}}{-7,4} \right)_{}$$ Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ . Substitute the values. $$y$$ of the second point minus $$y$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{4 - (-3)}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ . $$x$$ of the second point minus $$x$$ of the first point $$m = \frac{4 - (-3)}{-7 - (-2)}$$ . Simplify. $$\begin{array}{l} {m = \frac{7}{-5}} \\ {m = - \frac{7}{5}} \end{array}$$
Let’s verify this slope on the graph shown. $$\begin{array}{rll} m & = & \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } \\ m & = & \frac{-7}{5} \\ m & = & {- \frac{7}{5}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4.36
snippet: Example 4.36: Graph the line with y-intercept 2 whose slope is m = - \frac{2}{3} . Plot the given point, the y-intercept, (0,2) . Identify the rise and the run. m = - \frac{2}{3} \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } = \frac{-2}{3}...
body_xml:
Graph the line with y-intercept 2 whose slope is $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ . Plot the given point, the y-intercept, $$(0,2)$$ . Identify the rise and the run. $$m = - \frac{2}{3}$$ $$\frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } = \frac{-2}{3}$$ $$\text{rise} = -2$$ $$\text{run} = 3$$
Count the rise and the run. Mark the second point. Connect the two points with a line. You can check your work by finding a third point. title: Example 4.37
snippet: Example 4.37: Graph the line passing through the point \left( {-1,-3} \right) whose slope is m = 4. Plot the given point. Identify the rise and the run. m = 4 Write 4 as a fraction. \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} } = \frac{4}{1}...

Count the rise and run and mark the second point. Connect the two points with a line. You can check your work by finding a third point. Since the slope is $$m = 4$$ , it can be written as $$m = \frac{-4}{-1}$$ . Go back to $$(-1,-3)$$ and count out the rise, $$-4$$ , and the run, $$-1$$ .

title: Example 4.38
snippet: Example 4.38: The ‘pitch’ of a building’s roof is the slope of the roof. Knowing the pitch is important in climates where there is heavy snowfall. If the roof is too flat, the weight of the snow may cause it to collapse. What is the slope...
body_xml: The ‘pitch’ of a building’s roof is the slope of the roof. Knowing the pitch is important in climates where there is heavy snowfall. If the roof is too flat, the weight of the snow may cause it to collapse. What is the slope of the roof shown? Use the slope formula. $$m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }$$ Substitute the values for rise and run. $$m = \frac{9}{18}$$ Simplify. $$m = \frac{1}{2}$$ The slope of the roof is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . The roof rises 1 foot for every 2 feet of horizontal run.

title: Example 4.39
snippet: Example 4.39: Have you ever thought about the sewage pipes going from your house to the street? They must slope down \frac{1}{4} inch per foot in order to drain properly. What is the required slope? Use the slope formula. \begin{matrix} {m...
body_xml:
Have you ever thought about the sewage pipes going from your house to the street? They must slope down $$\frac{1}{4}$$ inch per foot in order to drain properly. What is the required slope? Use the slope formula. $$\begin{matrix} {m = \frac{ \text{rise} }{ \text{run} }} \\ {m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{inch} }{ \text{1 foot} }} \\ {m = \frac{- \frac{1}{4} \text{inch} }{ \text{12 inches} }} \end{matrix}$$ Simplify. $$m = - \frac{1}{48}$$ The slope of the pipe is $$- \frac{1}{48}$$ .
The pipe drops 1 inch for every 48 inches of horizontal run.

<note type="rule" source_type="Strategy for Choosing the Most Convenient Method to Graph a Line" title="Strategy for Choosing the Most Convenient Method to Graph a Line">
    <paragraph>Consider the form of the equation.</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>If it only has one variable, it is a vertical or horizontal line. $$x = a$$ is a vertical line passing through the x-axis at $$a$$ . $$y = b$$ is a horizontal line passing through the y-axis at $$b$$ .</item>
      <item>If $$y$$ is isolated on one side of the equation, in the form $$y = mx + b$$ , graph by using the slope and y-intercept. Identify the slope and y-intercept and then graph.</item>
      <item>If the equation is of the form $$Ax + By = C$$ , find the intercepts. Find the x- and y-intercepts, a third point, and then graph.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 4.49
snippet: Example 4.49: The equation F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32 is used to convert temperatures, C , on the Celsius scale to temperatures, F , on the Fahrenheit scale. ⓐ Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0. ⓑ Find the...
body_xml:
The equation $$F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$$ is used to convert temperatures, $$C$$ , on the Celsius scale to temperatures, $$F$$ , on the Fahrenheit scale. ⓐ Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0. ⓑ Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 20. ⓒ Interpret the slope and F-intercept of the equation. ⓓ Graph the equation. ⓐ Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0. Find $$F$$ when $$C = 0$$ . Simplify. $$\begin{array}{l} {F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32} \\ {F = \frac{9}{5}(0) + 32} \\ {F = 32} \end{array}$$ ⓑ Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 20. Find $$F$$ when $$C = 20$$ . Simplify. Simplify. $$\begin{array}{l} {F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32} \\ {F = \frac{9}{5}(20) + 32} \\ {F = 36 + 32} \\ {F = 68} \end{array}$$
ⓒ Interpret the slope and F-intercept of the equation. Even though this equation uses $$F$$ and $$C$$ , it is still in slope–intercept form. The slope, $$\frac{9}{5}$$ , means that the temperature Fahrenheit (F) increases 9 degrees when the temperature Celsius (C) increases 5 degrees. The F-intercept means that when the temperature is $$0^\circ$$ on the Celsius scale, it is $$32^\circ$$ on the Fahrenheit scale. ⓓ Graph the equation. We’ll need to use a larger scale than our usual. Start at the F-intercept $$\left( {0,32} \right)$$ then count out the rise of 9 and the run of 5 to get a second point. See Figure 4.26.

snippet: Example 4.50: Stella has a home business selling gourmet pizzas. The equation C = 4p + 25 models the relation between her weekly cost, C, in dollars and the number of pizzas, p, that she sells. ⓐ Find Stella’s cost for a week when she...
body_xml: Stella has a home business selling gourmet pizzas. The equation $$C = 4p + 25$$ models the relation between her weekly cost, C, in dollars and the number of pizzas, p, that she sells. ⓐ Find Stella’s cost for a week when she sells no pizzas. ⓑ Find the cost for a week when she sells 15 pizzas. ⓒ Interpret the slope and C-intercept of the equation. ⓓ Graph the equation. ⓐ Find Stella's cost for a week when she sells no pizzas. Find C when $$p = 0$$ . Simplify. Stella's fixed cost is \$25 when she sells no pizzas. ⓑ Find the cost for a week when she sells 15 pizzas. Find C when $$p = 15$$ . Simplify. Stella's costs are \$85 when she sells 15 pizzas. ⓒ Interpret the slope and C-intercept of the equation. The slope, 4, means that the cost increases by \$4 for each pizza Stella sells. The C-intercept means that even when Stella sells no pizzas, her costs for the week are \$25. ⓓ Graph the equation. We'll need to use a larger scale than our usual. Start at the C-intercept (0, 25) then count out the rise of 4 and the run of 1 to get a second point.

title: Example 4.51
snippet: Example 4.51: Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines 3x - 2y = 6 and y = \frac{3}{2}x + 1 are parallel. Solve the first equation for y . \begin{array}{rll} {3x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {- 2y} & = & {-3x + 6} \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & = &...
body_xml:
Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines $$3x - 2y = 6$$ and $$y = \frac{3}{2}x + 1$$ are parallel. Solve the first equation for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {3x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {- 2y} & = & {-3x + 6} \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & = & \frac{-3x + 6}{-2} \end{array}$$ and $$y = \frac{3}{2}x + 1$$ The equation is now in slope-intercept form. $$y = \frac{3}{2}x - 3$$ The equation of the second line is already in slope-intercept form. $$y = \frac{3}{2}x + 1$$ Identify the slope and $$y$$ -intercept of both lines. $$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ y & = & {\frac{3}{2}x - 3} \\ y & = & {mx + b} \\ m & = & \frac{3}{2} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{l} { y = \frac{3}{2}x + 1} \\ { y = mx + b} \\ {m = \frac{3}{2}} \end{array}$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, −3)}$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, 1)}$$
The lines have the same slope and different y-intercepts and so they are parallel. You may want to graph the lines to confirm whether they are parallel.

title: Example 4.52
snippet: Example 4.52: Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines y = -4 and y = 3 are parallel. \begin{array}{l} {y = -4} \\ {y = 0x - 4} \end{array} and \begin{array}{l} {y = 3} \\ {y = 0x + 3} \end{array} Write each equation in...
body_xml:
Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines $$y = -4$$ and $$y = 3$$ are parallel. $$\begin{array}{l} {y = -4} \\ {y = 0x - 4} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{array}{l} {y = 3} \\ {y = 0x + 3} \end{array}$$ Write each equation in slope-intercept form. $$y = 0x - 4$$ $$y = 0x + 3$$ Since there is no $$x$$ term we write $$0x$$ . $$y = mx + b$$ $$y = mx + b$$ Identify the slope and $$y$$ -intercept of both lines. $$m = 0$$ $$m = 0$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, 4)}$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, 3)}$$
The lines have the same slope and different y-intercepts and so they are parallel. There is another way you can look at this example. If you recognize right away from the equations that these are horizontal lines, you know their slopes are both 0. Since the horizontal lines cross the y-axis at $$y = -4$$ and at $$y = 3$$ , we know the y-intercepts are $$(0,-4)$$ and $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ . The lines have the same slope and different y-intercepts and so they are parallel.

unit_title: Use the Slope-Intercept Form of an Equation of a Line
title: Example 4.54
snippet: Example 4.54: Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines y = 2x - 3 and -6x + 3y = -9 are parallel. You may want to graph these lines, too, to see what they look like. y = 2x - 3 and -6x + 3y = -9 The first equation is already...
body_xml:
Use slopes and y-intercepts to determine if the lines $$y = 2x - 3$$ and $$-6x + 3y = -9$$ are parallel. You may want to graph these lines, too, to see what they look like. $$y = 2x - 3$$ and $$-6x + 3y = -9$$ The first equation is already in slope-intercept form. $$y = 2x - 3$$ Solve the second equation for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {- 6x + 3y} & = & -9 \\ {3y} & = & {6x - 9} \\ \frac{3y}{3} & = & \frac{6x - 9}{3} \\ y & = & {2x - 3} \end{array}$$ The second equation is now in slope-intercept form. $$y = 2x - 3$$ Identify the slope and $$y$$ -intercept of both lines. $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ y & = & {mx + b} \\ m & = & 2 \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ y & = & {mx + b} \\ m & = & 2 \end{array}$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, −3)}$$ $$y \text{-intercept is (0, −3)}$$
The lines have the same slope, but they also have the same y-intercepts. Their equations represent the same line. They are not parallel; they are the same line.

title: Example 4.55
snippet: Example 4.55: Use slopes to determine if the lines, y = -5x - 4 and x - 5y = 5 are perpendicular. The first equation is already in slope-intercept form. \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {-5x - 4} \end{array} Solve the second equation for y ....
body_xml:
Use slopes to determine if the lines, $$y = -5x - 4$$ and $$x - 5y = 5$$ are perpendicular. The first equation is already in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {-5x - 4} \end{array}$$ Solve the second equation for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rll} {x - 5y} & = & 5 \\ {- 5y} & = & {-x + 5} \\ \frac{-5y}{-5} & = & \frac{-x + 5}{-5} \\ y & = & {\frac{1}{5}x - 1} \end{array}$$ Identify the slope of each line. $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {-5x - 4} \\ y & = & {mx + b} \\ m_{1} & = & -5 \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{1}{5}x - 1} \\ y & = & {mx + b} \\ m_{2} & = & \frac{1}{5} \end{array}$$
The slopes are negative reciprocals of each other, so the lines are perpendicular. We check by multiplying the slopes, $$\begin{array}{l} {m_{1} \cdot m_{2}} \\ \\ {- 5\left( \frac{1}{5} \right)} \\ {- 1✓} \end{array}$$

Use slopes to determine if the lines, $$7x + 2y = 3$$ and $$2x + 7y = 5$$ are perpendicular. Solve the equations for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rllc} { 7x + 2y} & = & 3 & \\ { 2y} & = & {-7x + 3} & \\ { \frac{2y}{2}} & = & \frac{-7x + 3}{2} & \\ { y} & = & {- \frac{7}{2}x + \frac{3}{2}} & \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} {2x + 7y} & = & 5 \\ {7y} & = & {-2x + 5} \\ \frac{7y}{7} & = & \frac{-2x + 5}{7} \\ y & = & {- \frac{2}{7}x + \frac{5}{7}} \end{array}$$ Identify the slope of each line. $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {mx + b} \\ { m_{1}} & = & {- \frac{7}{2}} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {mx + b} \\ { m_{2}} & = & {- \frac{2}{7}} \end{array}$$
The slopes are reciprocals of each other, but they have the same sign. Since they are not negative reciprocals, the lines are not perpendicular.

Find an equation of a line that contains the points $$\left( {-2,4} \right)$$ and $$\left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ . Write the equation in slope–intercept form. Again, the first step will be to find the slope. Find the slope of the line through $$\left( {-2,4} \right) \text{and} \left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ . $$m = \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$ $$m = \frac{-3 - 4}{-2 - (-2)}$$ $$m = \frac{-7}{0}$$ The slope is undefined.
This tells us it is a vertical line. Both of our points have an x-coordinate of $$-2$$ . So our equation of the line is $$x = -2$$ . Since there is no $$y$$ , we cannot write it in slope–intercept form. You may want to sketch a graph using the two given points. Does the graph agree with our conclusion that this is a vertical line?

title: Example 4.67
snippet: Example 4.67: Find an equation of a line perpendicular to x = 5 that contains the point \left( {3,-2} \right) . Write the equation in slope–intercept form. Again, since we know one point, the point–slope option seems more promising than...
body_xml:
Find an equation of a line perpendicular to $$x = 5$$ that contains the point $$\left( {3,-2} \right)$$ . Write the equation in slope–intercept form. Again, since we know one point, the point–slope option seems more promising than the slope–intercept option. We need the slope to use this form, and we know the new line will be perpendicular to $$x = 5$$ . This line is vertical, so its perpendicular will be horizontal. This tells us the $$m_{ \text{⊥} } = 0$$ . Identify the point. $$\left( {3,-2} \right)$$ Identify the slope of the perpendicular line. $$m_{ \text{⊥} } = 0$$ Substitute the values into $$y - y_{1} = m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)$$ . $$\begin{matrix} {y - y_{1} = m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)} \\ {y - (-2) = 0\left( {x - 3} \right)} \\ {y + 2 = 0} \end{matrix}$$ Simplify. $$y = -2$$
Sketch the graph of both lines. Do they appear to be perpendicular?

title: Example 4.70
snippet: Example 4.70: The boundary line shown is y = 2x - 1 . Write the inequality shown by the graph. The line y = 2x - 1 is the boundary line. On one side of the line are the points with y > 2x - 1 and on the other side of the line are the...
body_xml:
<example number="4.70">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The boundary line shown is $$y = 2x - 1$$ . Write the inequality shown by the graph.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The line $$y = 2x - 1$$ is the boundary line. On one side of the line are the points with $$y > 2x - 1$$ and on the other side of the line are the points with $$y < 2x - 1$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let’s test the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and see which inequality describes its side of the boundary line.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>At $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which inequality is true:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {y > 2x - 1} & & \text{or} & & {y < 2x - 1?} \\ {y > 2x - 1} & & & & {y < 2x - 1} \\ {0\overset{?}{>}2 \cdot 0 - 1} & & & & {0\overset{?}{<}2 \cdot 0 - 1} \\ {0 > -1 \text{True} } & & & & {0 < -1 \text{False} } \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since, $$y > 2x - 1$$ is true, the side of the line with $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , is the solution. The shaded region shows the solution of the inequality $$y > 2x - 1$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the boundary line is graphed with a solid line, the inequality includes the equal sign.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The graph shows the inequality $$y \geq 2x - 1$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We could use any point as a test point, provided it is not on the line. Why did we choose $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ ? Because it’s the easiest to evaluate. You may want to pick a point on the other side of the boundary line and check that $$y < 2x - 1$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>Let’s test the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and see which inequality describes its side of the boundary line.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>At $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which inequality is true:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcccccrll} {2x + 3y} & > & 6 & & & \text{or} & & & {2x + 3y} & < & {6?} \\ {2x + 3y} & > & 6 & & & & & & {2x + 3y} & < & 6 \\ {2(0) + 3(0)} & \overset{?}{>} & 6 & & & & & & {2(0) + 3(0)} & \overset{?}{<} & 6 \\ 0 & > & {6 \text{False} } & & & & & & 0 & < & {6 \text{True} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So the side with $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is the side where $$2x + 3y < 6$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>(You may want to pick a point on the other side of the boundary line and check that $$2x + 3y > 6$$ .)</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the boundary line is graphed as a dashed line, the inequality does not include an equal sign.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The graph shows the solution to the inequality $$2x + 3y < 6$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 5.3
snippet: Example 5.3: Solve the system by graphing: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 2x + 1} \\ {y = 4x - 1} \end{array} \right.. Both of the equations in this system are in slope-intercept form, so we will use their slopes and y-intercepts to graph...
body_xml: Solve the system by graphing: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 2x + 1} \\ {y = 4x - 1} \end{array} \right..$$ Both of the equations in this system are in slope-intercept form, so we will use their slopes and y-intercepts to graph them. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 2x + 1} \\ {y = 4x - 1} \end{array} \right.$$ Find the slope and y-intercept of thefirst equation. Find the slope and y-intercept of thefirst equation. Graph the two lines. Determine the point of intersection. The lines intersect at (1, 3). Check the solution in both equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {2x + 1} \\ 3 & \overset{?}{=} & {2 \cdot 1 + 1} \\ 3 & = & {3 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {4x - 1} \\ 3 & \overset{?}{=} & {4 \cdot 1 - 1} \\ 3 & = & {3 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (1, 3).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Graphing
title: Example 5.4
snippet: Example 5.4: Solve the system by graphing: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + y = -1} \\ {2x + y = 0} \end{array} \right.. We’ll solve both of these equations for y so that we can easily graph them using their slopes and y-intercepts. \left\{...
body_xml: Solve the system by graphing: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + y = -1} \\ {2x + y = 0} \end{array} \right..$$ We’ll solve both of these equations for $$y$$ so that we can easily graph them using their slopes and y-intercepts. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + y = -1} \\ {2x + y = 0} \end{array} \right.$$ Solve the first equation for y.Find the slope and y-intercept.Solve the second equation for y.Find the slope and y-intercept. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {3x + y} & = & {- 1} \\ y & = & {- 3x - 1} \\ & & \\ m & = & {- 3} \\ b & = & {- 1} \\ & & \\ & & \\ {2x + y} & = & 0 \\ y & = & {- 2x} \\ & & \\ m & = & {- 2} \\ b & = & 0 \\ & & \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ Graph the lines. Determine the point of intersection. The lines intersect at (−1, 2). Check the solution in both equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {3x + y} & = & {- 1} \\ {3( - 1) + 2} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 1} \\ {- 1} & = & {- 1 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {2x + y} & = & 0 \\ {2( - 1) + 2} & \overset{?}{=} & 0 \\ 0 & = & {0 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (−1, 2).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Graphing
title: Example 5.5
snippet: Example 5.5: Solve the system by graphing: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = 2} \\ {x - y = 4} \end{array} \right.. We will find the x- and y-intercepts of both equations and use them to graph the lines. To find the intercepts, let x = 0...
body_xml: Solve the system by graphing: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = 2} \\ {x - y = 4} \end{array} \right..$$ We will find the x- and y-intercepts of both equations and use them to graph the lines. To find the intercepts, let x = 0 and solvefor y, then let y = 0 and solve for x. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{cll} {x + y} & = & 2 \\ {0 + y} & = & 2 \\ y & = & 2 \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{cll} {x + y} & = & 2 \\ {x + 0} & = & 2 \\ x & = & 2 \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ To find the intercepts, letx = 0 then let y = 0. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {x - y} & = & 4 \\ {0 - y} & = & 4 \\ {- y} & = & 4 \\ y & = & {- 4} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {x - y} & = & 4 \\ {x - 0} & = & 4 \\ x & = & 4 \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ Graph the line. Determine the point of intersection. The lines intersect at (3, −1). Check the solution in both equations. $$\begin{array}{cllccrll} {x + y} & = & 2 & & & {x - y} & = & 4 \\ {3 + (-1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 2 & & & {3 - (-1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 4 \\ 2 & = & {2✓} & & & 4 & = & {4✓} \end{array}$$ The solution is (3, −1).

snippet: Example 5.6: Solve the system by graphing: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 6} \\ {2x + 3y = 12} \end{array} \right.. We know the first equation represents a horizontalline whose y-intercept is 6. The second equation is most conveniently...

The second equation is most conveniently graphedusing intercepts. To find the intercepts, let x = 0 and then y = 0. Graph the lines. Determine the point of intersection. The lines intersect at (−3, 6). Check the solution to both equations. $$\begin{array}{cccccrll} y & = & 6 & & & {2x + 3y} & = & 12 \\ 6 & \overset{?}{=} & {6✓} & & & {2(-3) + 3(6)} & \overset{?}{=} & 12 \\ & & & & & {-6 + 18} & \overset{?}{=} & 12 \\ & & & & & 12 & = & {12✓} \end{array}$$ The solution is (−3, 6).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Graphing
title: Example 5.9
snippet: Example 5.9: Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 3x - 1} \\ {6x - 2y = 12} \end{array} \right.. We will compare the slopes and intercepts of the two...
body_xml:
Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 3x - 1} \\ {6x - 2y = 12} \end{array} \right..$$ We will compare the slopes and intercepts of the two lines. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = 3x - 1} \\ {6x - 2y = 12} \end{array} \right..$$ The first equation is already in slope-intercept form. $$y = 3x - 1$$ Write the second equation in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{rll} {6x - 2y} & = & 12 \\ {-2y} & = & {-6x + 12} \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & = & \frac{-6x + 12}{-2} \\ y & = & {3x - 6} \end{array}$$ Find the slope and intercept of each line. $$\begin{array}{rllcccrll} y & = & {3x - 1} & & & & y & = & {3x - 6} \\ m & = & 3 & & & & m & = & 3 \\ b & = & -1 & & & & b & = & -6 \end{array}$$ Since the slopes are the same and $$y$$ -intercepts are different, the lines are parallel.
A system of equations whose graphs are parallel lines has no solution and is inconsistent and independent.

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Graphing
title: Example 5.10
snippet: Example 5.10: Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = - 3} \\ {x - 5y = 5} \end{array} \right.. We will compare the slope and intercepts of the two...
body_xml:
Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = - 3} \\ {x - 5y = 5} \end{array} \right..$$ We will compare the slope and intercepts of the two lines. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = - 3} \\ {x - 5y = 5} \end{array} \right.$$ Write both equations in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {2x + y} & = & -3 \\ y & = & {-2x-3} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x - 5y = 5} & = & 5 \\ {-5y} & = & {-x + 5} \\ \frac{-5y}{-5} & = & \frac{-x + 5}{-5} \\ y & = & {\frac{1}{5}x - 1} \end{array}$$ Find the slope and intercept of each line. $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {-2x - 3} \\ m & = & -2 \\ b & = & -3 \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{1}{5}x - 1} \\ m & = & \frac{1}{5} \\ b & = & -1 \end{array}$$ Since the slopes are different, the lines intersect.
A system of equations whose graphs are intersect has 1 solution and is consistent and independent.

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Graphing
title: Example 5.11
snippet: Example 5.11: Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = 4} \\ {y = \frac{3}{2}x - 2} \end{array} \right. We will compare the slopes and intercepts of...
body_xml:
Without graphing, determine the number of solutions and then classify the system of equations. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = 4} \\ {y = \frac{3}{2}x - 2} \end{array} \right.$$ We will compare the slopes and intercepts of the two lines. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = 4} \\ {y = \frac{3}{2}x - 2} \end{array} \right.$$ Write the first equation in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{rll} {3x - 2y} & = & 4 \\ {-2y} & = & {-3x + 4} \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & = & \frac{-3x + 4}{-2} \\ y & = & {\frac{3}{2}x - 2} \end{array}$$ The second equation is already in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{r} {y = \frac{3}{2}x - 2} \end{array}$$ Since the slopes are the same, they have the same slope and same $$y$$ -intercept and so the lines are coincident.
A system of equations whose graphs are coincident lines has infinitely many solutions and is consistent and dependent.

title: Example 5.12
snippet: Example 5.12: Sondra is making 10 quarts of punch from fruit juice and club soda. The number of quarts of fruit juice is 4 times the number of quarts of club soda. How many quarts of fruit juice and how many quarts of club soda does Sondra...
body_xml:
<example number="5.12">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Sondra is making 10 quarts of punch from fruit juice and club soda. The number of quarts of fruit juice is 4 times the number of quarts of club soda. How many quarts of fruit juice and how many quarts of club soda does Sondra need?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. Read the problem.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. Identify what we are looking for.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We are looking for the number of quarts of fruit juice and the number of quarts of club soda that Sondra will need.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose variables to represent those quantities.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$f =$$ number of quarts of fruit juice. $$c =$$ number of quarts of club soda</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4. Translate into a system of equations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We now have the system. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {f + c = 10} \\ {f = 4c} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5. Solve the system of equations using good algebra techniques.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The point of intersection (2, 8) is the solution. This means Sondra needs 2 quarts of club soda and 8 quarts of fruit juice.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Does this make sense in the problem?</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Yes, the number of quarts of fruit juice, 8 is 4 times the number of quarts of club soda, 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Yes, 10 quarts of punch is 8 quarts of fruit juice plus 2 quarts of club soda.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Sondra needs 8 quarts of fruit juice and 2 quarts of soda.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 5.14
snippet: Example 5.14: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = -1} \\ {y = x + 5} \end{array} \right. The second equation is already solved for y. We will substitute the expression in place of y in the first equation....
body_xml: Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = -1} \\ {y = x + 5} \end{array} \right.$$ The second equation is already solved for y. We will substitute the expression in place of y in the first equation. The second equation is already solved for y.We will substitute into the first equation. Replace the y with x + 5. Solve the resulting equation for x. Substitute x = −3 into y = x + 5 to find y. The ordered pair is (−3, 2). Check the ordered pair in both equations: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {x + y} & = & {- 1} \\ {- 3 + 2} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 1} \\ {- 1} & = & {- 1 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {x + 5} \\ 2 & \overset{?}{=} & {- 3 + 5} \\ 2 & = & {2 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (−3, 2).

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.15
snippet: Example 5.15: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + y = 5} \\ {2x + 4y = -10} \end{array} \right. We need to solve one equation for one variable. Then we will substitute that expression into the other equation....
body_xml: Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + y = 5} \\ {2x + 4y = -10} \end{array} \right.$$ We need to solve one equation for one variable. Then we will substitute that expression into the other equation. Solve for y.Substitute into the other equation. Replace the y with −3x + 5. Solve the resulting equation for x. Substitute x = 3 into 3x + y = 5 to find y. The ordered pair is (3, −4). Check the ordered pair in both equations: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {3x + y} & = & 5 \\ {3 \cdot 3 + ( - 4)} & \overset{?}{=} & 5 \\ {9 - 4} & \overset{?}{=} & 5 \\ 5 & = & {5 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {2x + 4y} & = & {- 10} \\ {2 \cdot 3 + 4( - 4)} & = & {- 10} \\ {6 - 16} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 10} \\ {- 10} & = & {- 10 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (3, −4).

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.16
snippet: Example 5.16: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x - 2y = -2} \\ {3x + 2y = 34} \end{array} \right. We will solve the first equation for x and then substitute the expression into the second equation. Solve for...
body_xml: Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x - 2y = -2} \\ {3x + 2y = 34} \end{array} \right.$$ We will solve the first equation for $$x$$ and then substitute the expression into the second equation. Solve for x.Substitute into the other equation. Replace the x with 2y − 2. Solve the resulting equation for y. Substitute y = 5 into x − 2y = −2 to find x. The ordered pair is (8, 5). Check the ordered pair in both equations: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {x - 2y} & = & {- 2} \\ {8 - 2 \cdot 5} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 2} \\ {8 - 10} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 2} \\ {- 2} & = & {- 2 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {3x + 2y} & = & 34 \\ {3 \cdot 8 + 2 \cdot 5} & \overset{?}{=} & 34 \\ {24 + 10} & \overset{?}{=} & 34 \\ 34 & = & {34 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (8, 5).

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.17
snippet: Example 5.17: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = -2x + 5} \\ {y = \frac{1}{2}x} \end{array} \right. Since both equations are solved for y, we can substitute one into the other. Substitute \frac{1}{2}x for y in...
body_xml: Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = -2x + 5} \\ {y = \frac{1}{2}x} \end{array} \right.$$ Since both equations are solved for y, we can substitute one into the other. Substitute $$\frac{1}{2}x$$ for y in the first equation. Replace the y with $$\frac{1}{2}x.$$ Solve the resulting equation. Startby clearing the fraction. Solve for x. Substitute x = 2 into y = $$\frac{1}{2}x$$ to find y. The ordered pair is (2,1). Check the ordered pair in both equations: $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {\frac{1}{2}x} \\ 1 & \overset{?}{=} & {\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2} \\ 1 & = & {1 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {- 2x + 5} \\ 1 & \overset{?}{=} & {- 2 \cdot 2 + 5} \\ 1 & = & {- 4 + 5} \\ 1 & = & {1 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (2,1).

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.18
snippet: Example 5.18: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x + 2y = 4} \\ {6x - y = 8} \end{array} \right. We need to solve one equation for one variable. We will solve the first equation for y. Solve the first equation for...
body_xml: Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x + 2y = 4} \\ {6x - y = 8} \end{array} \right.$$ We need to solve one equation for one variable. We will solve the first equation for y. Solve the first equation for y. Substitute −2x + 2 for y in the second equation. Replace the y with −2x + 2. Solve the equation for x. Substitute $$x = \frac{5}{4}$$ into 4x + 2y = 4 to find y. The ordered pair is $$\left( {\frac{5}{4}, - \frac{1}{2}} \right).$$ Check the ordered pair in both equations. $$\begin{array}{lccl} \begin{array}{rll} {4x + 2y} & = & 4 \\ {4\left( \frac{5}{4} \right) + 2\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 4 \\ {5 - 1} & \overset{?}{=} & 4 \\ 4 & = & {4 ✓} \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {6x - y} & = & 8 \\ {6\left( \frac{5}{4} \right) - \left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 8 \\ {\frac{15}{4} - \left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 8 \\ \frac{16}{2} & \overset{?}{=} & 8 \\ 8 & = & {8 ✓} \end{array} \end{array}$$ The solution is $$\left( {\frac{5}{4}, - \frac{1}{2}} \right).$$

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.19
snippet: Example 5.19: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x - 3y = 6} \\ {15y - 20x = -30} \end{array} \right. We need to solve one equation for one variable. We will solve the first equation for x. Solve the first...
body_xml:
Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x - 3y = 6} \\ {15y - 20x = -30} \end{array} \right.$$ We need to solve one equation for one variable. We will solve the first equation for x. Solve the first equation for x. Substitute $$\frac{3}{4}y + \frac{3}{2}$$ for x in the second equation. Replace the x with $$\frac{3}{4}y + \frac{3}{2}.$$ Solve for y.
Since 0 = 0 is a true statement, the system is consistent. The equations are dependent. The graphs of these two equations would give the same line. The system has infinitely many solutions.

unit_title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution
title: Example 5.20
snippet: Example 5.20: Solve the system by substitution. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {5x - 2y = -10} \\ {y = \frac{5}{2}x} \end{array} \right. The second equation is already solved for y, so we can substitute for y in the first equation. Substitute x...
body_xml:
Solve the system by substitution. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {5x - 2y = -10} \\ {y = \frac{5}{2}x} \end{array} \right.$$ The second equation is already solved for y, so we can substitute for y in the first equation. Substitute x for y in the first equation. Replace the y with $$\frac{5}{2}x.$$ Solve for x.
Since 0 = −10 is a false statement the equations are inconsistent. The graphs of the two equation would be parallel lines. The system has no solutions.

Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Let $$n =$$ the first numberLet $$m =$$ the second number Step 4. Translate into a system of equations. The sum of two numbers is zero. body_xml: The perimeter of a rectangle is 88. The length is five more than twice the width. Find the length and the width. Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what you are looking for. title: Example 5.24
snippet: Example 5.24: Heather has been offered two options for her salary as a trainer at the gym. Option A would pay her \$25,000 plus \$15 for each training session. Option B would pay her \$10,000 + \$40 for each training session. How many...
body_xml: Heather has been offered two options for her salary as a trainer at the gym. Option A would pay her \$25,000 plus \$15 for each training session. Option B would pay her \$10,000 + \$40 for each training session. How many training sessions would make the salary options equal? Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what you are looking for. We are looking for the number of training sessionsthat would make the pay equal. Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Let $$s =$$ Heather’s salary. $$n =$$ the number of training sessions Step 4. Translate into a system of equations. Option A would pay her \$25,000 plus \$15for each training session. Option B would pay her \$10,000 + \$40for each training session The system is: Step 5. Solve the system of equations.We will use substitution. Substitute 25,000 + 15n for s in the second equation. Solve for n. Step 6. Check the answer. Are 600 training sessions a year reasonable?Are the two options equal when n = 600? Step 7. Answer the question. The salary options would be equal for 600 training sessions.

    <heading level="4">How to solve a system of equations by elimination.</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Step 1. Write both equations in standard form. If any coefficients are fractions, clear them.</item>
      <item>Step 2. Make the coefficients of one variable opposites. Decide which variable you will eliminate. Multiply one or both equations so that the coefficients of that variable are opposites.</item>
      <item>Step 3. Add the equations resulting from Step 2 to eliminate one variable.</item>
      <item>Step 4. Solve for the remaining variable.</item>
      <item>Step 5. Substitute the solution from Step 4 into one of the original equations. Then solve for the other variable.</item>

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.26
snippet: Example 5.26: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = 10} \\ {x - y = 12} \end{array} \right. Both equations are in standard form. The coefficients of y are already opposites. Add the two equations to eliminate...
body_xml: Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = 10} \\ {x - y = 12} \end{array} \right.$$ Both equations are in standard form. The coefficients of y are already opposites. Add the two equations to eliminate y.The resulting equation has only 1 variable, x. Solve for x, the remaining variable.Substitute x = 11 into one of the original equations. Solve for the other variable, y. Write the solution as an ordered pair. The ordered pair is (11, −1). Check that the ordered pair is a solutionto both original equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {x + y} & = & 10 \\ {11 + \left( {- 1} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 10 \\ 10 & = & {10 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {x - y} & = & 12 \\ {11 - \left( {- 1} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 12 \\ 12 & = & {12 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (11, −1).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.27
snippet: Example 5.27: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = -2} \\ {5x - 6y = 10} \end{array} \right. Both equations are in standard form. None of the coefficients are opposites. We can make the coefficients of y...
body_xml: Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x - 2y = -2} \\ {5x - 6y = 10} \end{array} \right.$$ Both equations are in standard form. None of the coefficients are opposites. We can make the coefficients of y opposites by multiplyingthe first equation by −3. Simplify. Add the two equations to eliminate y. Solve for the remaining variable, x.Substitute x = −4 into one of the original equations. Solve for y. Write the solution as an ordered pair. The ordered pair is (−4, −5). Check that the ordered pair is a solution toboth original equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {3x - 2y} & = & {- 2} \\ {3\left( {- 4} \right) - 2\left( {- 5} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 2} \\ {- 12 + 10} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 2} \\ {- 2y} & = & {- 2 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {5x - 6y} & = & 10 \\ {3\left( {- 4} \right) - 6\left( {- 5} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 10 \\ {- 20 + 30} & \overset{?}{=} & 10 \\ 10 & = & {10 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (−4, −5).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.28
snippet: Example 5.28: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x - 3y = 9} \\ {7x + 2y = -6} \end{array} \right. In this example, we cannot multiply just one equation by any constant to get opposite coefficients. So we will...
body_xml:
Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {4x - 3y = 9} \\ {7x + 2y = -6} \end{array} \right.$$ In this example, we cannot multiply just one equation by any constant to get opposite coefficients. So we will strategically multiply both equations by a constant to get the opposites. Both equations are in standard form. To get oppositecoefficients of y, we will multiply the first equation by 2and the second equation by 3. Simplify. Add the two equations to eliminate y. Solve for x.Substitute x = 0 into one of the original equations. Solve for y. Write the solution as an ordered pair. The ordered pair is (0, −3). Check that the ordered pair is a solution toboth original equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {4x - 3y} & = & 9 \\ {4(0) - 3\left( {- 3} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & 9 \\ 9 & = & {9 ✓} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {7x + 2y} & = & {- 6} \\ {7(0) + 2\left( {- 3} \right)} & \overset{?}{=} & {- 6} \\ {- 6} & = & {- 6 ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (0, −3).
What other constants could we have chosen to eliminate one of the variables? Would the solution be the same?

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.29
snippet: Example 5.29: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + \frac{1}{2}y = 6} \\ {\frac{3}{2}x + \frac{2}{3}y = \frac{17}{2}} \end{array} \right. In this example, both equations have fractions. Our first step will be to...
body_xml: Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + \frac{1}{2}y = 6} \\ {\frac{3}{2}x + \frac{2}{3}y = \frac{17}{2}} \end{array} \right.$$ In this example, both equations have fractions. Our first step will be to multiply each equation by its LCD to clear the fractions. To clear the fractions, multiply each equation by its LCD. Simplify. Now we are ready to eliminate one of the variables. Notice thatboth equations are in standard form. We can eliminate y multiplying the top equation by −4. Simplify and add.Substitute x = 3 into one of the original equations. Solve for y. Write the solution as an ordered pair. The ordered pair is (3, 6). Check that the ordered pair is a solutionto both original equations. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rll} {x + \frac{1}{2}y} & = & 6 \\ {3 + \frac{1}{2}(6)} & \overset{?}{=} & 6 \\ {3 + 3} & \overset{?}{=} & 6 \\ 6 & = & {6 ✓} \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \\ & & \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {\frac{3}{2}x + \frac{2}{3}y} & = & \frac{17}{2} \\ {\frac{3}{2}(3) + \frac{2}{3}(6)} & \overset{?}{=} & \frac{17}{2} \\ {\frac{9}{2} + 4} & \overset{?}{=} & \frac{17}{2} \\ {\frac{9}{2} + \frac{8}{2}} & \overset{?}{=} & \frac{17}{2} \\ \frac{17}{2} & = & {\frac{17}{2} ✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is (3, 6).

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.30
snippet: Example 5.30: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 4y = 12} \\ {y = 3 - \frac{3}{4}x} \end{array} \right. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 4y = 12} \\ {y = 3 - \frac{3}{4}x} \end{array} \right. Write the second...
body_xml:
Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 4y = 12} \\ {y = 3 - \frac{3}{4}x} \end{array} \right.$$ $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 4y = 12} \\ {y = 3 - \frac{3}{4}x} \end{array} \right.$$ Write the second equation in standard form. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {3x + 4y} & = & 12 \\ {\frac{3}{4}x + y} & = & 3 \end{array} \right.$$ Clear the fractions by multiplying the second equation by 4. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {3x + 4y} & = & 12 \\ {4\left( {\frac{3}{4}x + y} \right)} & = & {4(3)} \end{array} \right.$$ Simplify. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {3x + 4y} & = & 12 \\ {3x + 4y} & = & 12 \end{array} \right.$$ To eliminate a variable, we multiply the second equation by $$-1$$ . Simplify and add. $$\begin{matrix} { \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {3x+4y} & = & 12 \\ {-3x-4y} & = & -12 \end{array} \right.}} \\ {0 = 0} \end{matrix}$$
This is a true statement. The equations are consistent but dependent. Their graphs would be the same line. The system has infinitely many solutions. After we cleared the fractions in the second equation, did you notice that the two equations were the same? That means we have coincident lines.

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.31
snippet: Example 5.31: Solve the system by elimination. \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {-6x + 15y = 10} \\ {2x - 5y = -5} \end{array} \right. The equations are in standard form. \left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {- 6x + 15y} & = & 10 \\ {2x - 5y} & = & -5...
body_xml:
Solve the system by elimination. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {-6x + 15y = 10} \\ {2x - 5y = -5} \end{array} \right.$$ The equations are in standard form. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {- 6x + 15y} & = & 10 \\ {2x - 5y} & = & -5 \end{array} \right.$$ Multiply the second equation by 3 to eliminate a variable. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {- 6x + 15y} & = & 10 \\ {3\left( {2x - 5y} \right)} & = & {3(-5)} \end{array} \right.$$ Simplify and add. $$\begin{matrix} \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\left\{ \begin{array}{rll} {-6x+15y} & = & { 10} \\ {6x-15y} & = & -15 \end{array} \right.} \\ {0 \neq -5} \end{matrix}$$
This statement is false. The equations are inconsistent and so their graphs would be parallel lines. The system does not have a solution.

unit_title: Solve Systems of Equations by Elimination
title: Example 5.32
snippet: Example 5.32: The sum of two numbers is 39. Their difference is 9. Find the numbers. Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for two numbers. Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a...
body_xml: The sum of two numbers is 39. Their difference is 9. Find the numbers. Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for two numbers. Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Choose a variable to represent that quantity. Let $$n =$$ the first number. $$m =$$ the second number. Step 4. Translate into a system of equations. The system is: The sum of two numbers is 39. $$n + m = 39$$ Their difference is 9. $$\begin{matrix} {n - m = 9} \\ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {n + m = 39} \\ {n - m = 9} \end{array} \right. \end{matrix}$$ Step 5. Solve the system of equations. To solve the system of equations, use elimination. The equations are in standard form and the coefficients of $$m$$ are opposites. Add. Solve for $$n$$ . Substitute $$n = 24$$ into one of the original equations and solve for $$m$$ . $$\begin{matrix} \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {n+m=39} \\ {n-m=9} \end{array} \right.} \\ {2n = 48} \\ \\ { n = 24} \\ {n + m = 39} \\ {24 + m = 39} \\ {m = 15} \end{matrix}$$ Step 6. Check the answer. Since $$24 + 15 = 39$$ and $$24 - 15 = 9$$ , the answers check. Step 7. Answer the question. The numbers are 24 and 15.

Solve for s. Substitute s = 140 into one of the originalequations and then solve for f. Step 6. Check the answer. Verify that these numbers make sensein the problem and that they aresolutions to both equations.We leave this to you! Step 7. Answer the question. body_xml:
<example number="5.34">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each system of linear equations decide whether it would be more convenient to solve it by substitution or elimination. Explain your answer.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>ⓐ $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 8y = 40} \\ {7x - 4y = -32} \end{array} \right.$$ ⓑ $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {5x + 6y = 12} \\ {y = \frac{2}{3}x - 1} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>ⓐ $$\begin{array}{ccl} & & \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {3x + 8y = 40} \\ {7x - 4y = -32} \end{array} \right. \end{array}$$ Since both equations are in standard form, using elimination will be most convenient.</item>
        <item>ⓑ $$\begin{array}{ccl} & & \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {5x + 6y = 12} \\ {y = \frac{2}{3}x - 1} \end{array} \right. \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>>Since one equation is already solved for y, using substitution will be most convenient.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Translate to a system of equations: A married couple together earns \$110,000 a year. The wife earns \$16,000 less than twice what her husband earns. What does the husband earn? We are looking for the amount that the husband and wife each earn. Let $$h =$$ the amount the husband earns. $$w =$$ the amount the wife earns. Translate. A married couple together earns \$110,000. $$w + h = 110,000$$ The wife earns \$16,000 less than twice what husband earns. $$w = 2h - 16,000$$ The system of equations is: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {w + h = 110,000} \\ {w = 2h - 16,000} \end{array} \right.$$

body_xml: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: The difference of two complementary angles is 26 degrees. Find the measures of the angles. Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for the measure of each angle. Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Let $$x =$$ the measure of the first angle $$x =$$ . $$m =$$ the measure of the second angle. Step 4. Translate into a system of equations. The angles are complementary. $$x + y = 90$$ The difference of the two angles is 26 degrees. $$x - y = 26$$ The system is $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x + y = 90} \\ {x - y = 26} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 5. Solve the system of equations by elimination. $$\begin{array}{l} \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x+y=90} \\ {x-y=26} \end{array} \right.} \\ {2x = 116} \end{array}$$ Substitute $$x = 58$$ into the first equation. $$\begin{array}{rll} {x + y} & = & 90 \\ {58 + y} & = & 90 \\ y & = & 32 \end{array}$$ Step 6. Check the answer in the problem. $$\begin{matrix} {58 + 32 = 90✓} \\ {58 - 32 = 26✓} \end{matrix}$$ Step 7. Answer the question. The angle measures are 58 degrees and 32 degrees.

snippet: Example 5.41: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: Randall has 125 feet of fencing to enclose the rectangular part of his backyard adjacent to his house. He will only need to fence around three sides, because the fourth side...
body_xml: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: Randall has 125 feet of fencing to enclose the rectangular part of his backyard adjacent to his house. He will only need to fence around three sides, because the fourth side will be the wall of the house. He wants the length of the fenced yard (parallel to the house wall) to be 5 feet more than four times as long as the width. Find the length and the width. Step 1. Read the problem. Step 2. Identify what you are looking for. We are looking for the length and width. Step 3. Name what we are looking for. Let $$L =$$ the length of the fenced yard. $$W =$$ the width of the fenced yard Step 4. Translate into a system of equations. One length and two widths equal 125. The length will be 5 feet more than four times the width. The system is:Step 5. Solve the system of equations by substitution. Substitute L = 4W + 5 into the firstequation, then solve for W. Substitute 20 for W in the secondequation, then solve for L. Step 6. Check the answer in the problem. $$\begin{array}{rll} {20 + 28 + 20} & = & {125 ✓} \\ 85 & = & {4 \cdot 20 + 5 ✓} \end{array}$$ Step 7. Answer the equation. The length is 85 feet and the width is 20 feet.

title: Example 5.42
snippet: Example 5.42: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: Joni left St. Louis on the interstate, driving west towards Denver at a speed of 65 miles per hour. Half an hour later, Kelly left St. Louis on the same route as Joni,...
body_xml: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: Joni left St. Louis on the interstate, driving west towards Denver at a speed of 65 miles per hour. Half an hour later, Kelly left St. Louis on the same route as Joni, driving 78 miles per hour. How long will it take Kelly to catch up to Joni? A diagram is useful in helping us visualize the situation. Identify and name what we are looking for.A chart will help us organize the data.We know the rates of both Joni and Kelly, and sowe enter them in the chart. We are looking for the length of time Kelly,k, and Joni, j, will each drive.Since $$D = r \cdot t$$ we can fill in the Distance column. Translate into a system of equations.To make the system of equations, we must recognize that Kelly and Joni will drive the same distance. So, $$65j = 78k.$$ Also, since Kelly left later, her time will be $$\frac{1}{2}$$ hour less than Joni’s time.So, $$k = j - \frac{1}{2}.$$ Now we have the system. Solve the system of equations by substitution. Substitute $$k = j - \frac{1}{2}$$ into the second equation, then solve for j. To find Kelly’s time, substitute j = 3 into the first equation, then solve for k. Check the answer in the problem. Joni 3 hours (65 mph) = 195 miles. Kelly $$2\frac{1}{2}$$ hours (78 mph) = 195 miles. Yes, they will have traveled the same distancewhen they meet. Answer the question. Kelly will catch up to Joni in $$2\frac{1}{2}$$ hours.By then, Joni will have traveled 3 hours.

title: Example 5.43
snippet: Example 5.43: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: A river cruise ship sailed 60 miles downstream for 4 hours and then took 5 hours sailing upstream to return to the dock. Find the speed of the ship in still water and the...
body_xml: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: A river cruise ship sailed 60 miles downstream for 4 hours and then took 5 hours sailing upstream to return to the dock. Find the speed of the ship in still water and the speed of the river current. Read the problem. This is a uniform motion problem and a picture will help us visualize the situation. Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for the speed of the shipin still water and the speed of the current. Name what we are looking for. Let $$s =$$ the rate of the ship in still water. $$c =$$ the rate of the current A chart will help us organize the information.The ship goes downstream and then upstream.Going downstream, the current helps theship; therefore, the ship’s actual rate is s + c.Going upstream, the current slows the ship;therefore, the actual rate is s − c. Downstream it takes 4 hours.Upstream it takes 5 hours.Each way the distance is 60 miles. Translate into a system of equations.Since rate times time is distance, we canwrite the system of equations. Solve the system of equations.Distribute to put both equations in standardform, then solve by elimination. Multiply the top equation by 5 and the bottom equation by 4.Add the equations, then solve for s. Substitute s = 13.5 into one of the original equations. Check the answer in the problem. The downstream rate would be 13.5 + 1.5 = 15 mph. In 4 hours the ship would travel 15 · 4 = 60 miles. The upstream rate would be 13.5 − 1.5 = 12 mph. In 5 hours the ship would travel 12 · 5 = 60 miles. Answer the question. The rate of the ship is 13.5 mph andthe rate of the current is 1.5 mph.

title: Example 5.44
snippet: Example 5.44: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: A private jet can fly 1095 miles in three hours with a tailwind but only 987 miles in three hours into a headwind. Find the speed of the jet in still air and the speed of the...
body_xml: Translate to a system of equations and then solve: A private jet can fly 1095 miles in three hours with a tailwind but only 987 miles in three hours into a headwind. Find the speed of the jet in still air and the speed of the wind. Read the problem. This is a uniform motion problem and a picture will help us visualize. Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for the speed of the jetin still air and the speed of the wind. Name what we are looking for. Let $$j =$$ the speed of the jet in still air. $$w =$$ the speed of the wind A chart will help us organize the information.The jet makes two trips-one in a tailwindand one in a headwind.In a tailwind, the wind helps the jet and sothe rate is j + w.In a headwind, the wind slows the jet andso the rate is j − w. Each trip takes 3 hours.In a tailwind the jet flies 1095 miles.In a headwind the jet flies 987 miles. Translate into a system of equations.Since rate times time is distance, we get thesystem of equations. Solve the system of equations.Distribute, then solve by elimination. Add, and solve for j.Substitute j = 347 into one of the originalequations, then solve for w. Check the answer in the problem. With the tailwind, the actual rate of the jet would be 347 + 18 = 365 mph. In 3 hours the jet would travel 365 · 3 = 1095 miles. Going into the headwind, the jet’s actual rate would be 347 − 18 = 329 mph. In 3 hours the jet would travel 329 · 3 = 987 miles. Answer the question. The rate of the jet is 347 mph and therate of the wind is 18 mph.
